summary: Hybrid key exchange combines several key exchange algorithms so a connection stays secure as long as at least one of them holds. It is motivated by the move to post-quantum cryptography. This Informational document provides a construction for hybrid key exchange in TLS 1.3.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9954 describes how TLS 1.3 can combine two or more key-exchange algorithms into one negotiated group. The combined session secret is intended to remain secure as long as one component algorithm remains unbroken.

subtitle: A TLS 1.3 construction that combines multiple key-exchange algorithms.

tldr.problem: Users may want protection against future breaks in a traditional key-exchange algorithm while also using a newer algorithm whose security is less studied. Recorded encrypted sessions could be exposed if their key exchange is later broken.
tldr.mechanism: Each algorithm combination is negotiated as a NamedGroup. The component public keys or ciphertexts are concatenated in a fixed order, and the component shared secrets are concatenated for input to the TLS 1.3 key schedule.
tldr.outcome: The construction aims to keep the resulting secret secure if at least one component remains unbroken. It requires fixed-length component values and does not choose the algorithms to combine.

today: RFC 9954 is an Informational document, published July 2026, that describes hybrid key exchange in TLS 1.3. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Hybrid key exchange uses multiple algorithms based on different cryptographic assumptions and combines their results. RFC 9954 gives a construction for hybrid ephemeral key exchange in TLS 1.3. Its primary goal is for the final shared secret to remain secure if at least one component algorithm remains unbroken.

The RFC is motivated in part by the transition to post-quantum cryptography and by the possibility that an attacker records encrypted traffic for later decryption. It does not select particular next-generation algorithms or define their identifiers. It also does not cover authentication using next-generation algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes how TLS 1.3 can use several key-exchange algorithms together. It does not decide which algorithms should be combined.

sections.title: Key Encapsulation Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC describes key exchange using a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM). A KEM has a key-generation operation that produces a public and secret key, an encapsulation operation that produces a ciphertext and shared secret, and a decapsulation operation that recovers the shared secret.

TLS 1.3 implementations may reuse ephemeral public keys, so any KEM used in this construction must be designed to remain secure when a public key is reused. Implementations that reuse a key must stay within the KEM's reuse limits, and they must not reuse randomness when creating KEM ciphertexts.
sections.plainLanguage: A KEM lets one party create a shared secret using the other party's public key. A KEM used here must account for possible public-key reuse and use fresh randomness for ciphertext generation.

sections.title: Negotiating the Algorithm Combination
sections.content:
Each combination of algorithms has its own NamedGroup identifier and is offered through the TLS 1.3 supported-groups extension. The identifier is an opaque value; it does not encode an internal grammar. Each hybrid identifier corresponds to an ordered combination of two or more algorithms.

A client and server that support the same hybrid group can negotiate it through TLS 1.3 mechanisms. The RFC also describes compatibility goals for exchanges involving an endpoint that is not hybrid-aware, where the parties may use a non-hybrid key exchange if they are willing to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: Each algorithm combination has a single group name for negotiation. The name identifies the combination, and the order of its algorithms is defined by that group.

sections.title: Sending the Component Key Values
sections.content:
The construction concatenates the component public keys or ciphertexts into one TLS KeyShareEntry value. It adds no length fields or other encoding between components, so each component's representation and length must be fixed once its algorithm is selected. The concatenated components must follow the order defined by the NamedGroup.

The key_exchange field is limited to 2^16-1 bytes. A ClientHello may exceed one packet when it carries large post-quantum keys. If a client offers multiple combinations that share a component algorithm, the same component key value may be reused within that ClientHello, but values for different algorithms must be independently generated.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server join component key values in the order named by the negotiated group. Because the encoding has no length markers between values, each component must have a fixed length.

sections.title: Combining the Shared Secrets
sections.content:
The shared secrets produced by the component algorithms are concatenated in the same order as the algorithms in the NamedGroup. The combined value replaces the usual (EC)DHE shared secret as input to the TLS 1.3 key schedule, where it is processed by HKDF-Extract.

The construction assumes the component shared secrets have fixed lengths once the group is selected. Variable-length secrets could make the concatenation ambiguous and could create timing or other security risks during key derivation.
sections.plainLanguage: The component shared secrets are placed one after another in a defined order. TLS then uses that combined value in its existing key schedule.

sections.title: Security Conditions and Limits
sections.content:
The security goal depends on the combined secret retaining the hybrid property: it remains secure if at least one component key exchange algorithm is unbroken. The RFC discusses this property for fixed-length shared secrets and notes assumptions about the hash function used by the key schedule.

Public keys, ciphertexts, and shared secrets must have fixed lengths once an algorithm is chosen. The RFC warns that variable-length secret processing can create timing side channels and can create risks if the key-derivation hash loses collision resistance. The construction must be used only with algorithms that provide fixed-length shared secrets.
sections.plainLanguage: The construction depends on at least one component remaining secure and on fixed-length values. Variable lengths can make secret processing ambiguous or expose information through timing.

viz.caption: Goals listed for hybrid key exchange in RFC 9954

items.title: Security
items.text: The shared secret should remain secure if one component remains unbroken.

items.title: Compatibility
items.text: Hybrid-aware endpoints should be able to communicate with non-hybrid-aware endpoints.

items.title: Latency
items.text: Negotiation should not add round trips.

items.title: Duplicate data
items.text: Offers should avoid sending repeated public keys when possible.
